body:
I like this a lot. This allows to await a threadded resource finishing without breaking changes and it is pretty easy to write with gdscript:

```gdscript
signal loaded

func loader():
   ResourceLoader.load_threaded("filepath", loaded.emit)
   await loaded
   add_child(ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get("filepath").instanciate()
```

When I first read this, I intuitively assumed it would be an addition to `load_threaded_request`.

I think adding one more optional argument to that method would be the better way to go about this. Especially as I would assume it to be working similar to an async version of `load`.

I also do not understand the upside of moving this into its own function over giving` loead_threaded_request` an additional argument. I think this is more confusing and hawing two functions doing basically the same adds more maintenance work.

Could you elaborate if there's an upside to making this its own thing?

[edit: rephrased a gut-response to be more professional]

> Could you elaborate if there's an upside to making this its own thing?

1) It's either breaking change (shifting other optional arguments) or `load_threaded_request(path, "", false, ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_REUSE, _on_loaded)` in the simplest case.
2) I like the idea of having two options: a default, set-and-forget `load_threaded` function, and the older function triplet for when more control is needed, including blocking wait.
3) Now `load_threaded_request` marks the beginning of a request and `load_threaded_get` marks the end of it. And I believe it feels more natural to have a separate `do_the_thing` function rather than expecting for "end" to be called manually only if some argument wasn't provided to "begin". Especially when you have to explain it briefly in documentation.

We were working on making whitelisted variants of this, so @fire (me) and @lyuma would like to take a review.

We've had some experience tracing how the code works.

https://github.com/V-Sekai/godot/commits/resource-loader-whitelist-prev-4.5

1. We can't do breaking changes so it'll be the second option.

> load_threaded_request(path, "", false, ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_REUSE, _on_loaded) in the simplest case.

2. I think @smix8 explained it best to have a high level api and an low level api (avoid making middle level apis).

> I like the idea of having two options: a default, set-and-forget load_threaded function, and the older function triplet for when more control is needed, including blocking wait.

3. Can you explain this with an example?

Just to clarify, my previous list was meant to justify adding a separate `load_threaded` method instead of adding optional argument to `load_threaded_request` as it was questioned.

## 1.
Let me rephrase it then: as breaking changes are not allowed, for the simplest case we have two options:
- `load_threaded(path, _on_loaded)` with the separate method
- `load_threaded_request(path, "", false, ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_REUSE, _on_loaded)` with additional argument

I lean towards the first, as it is much cleaner, which is important if we want it to be used often.

## 3.
Internally, each `LoadToken` tracks the user request balance via the `user_rc` variable: incremented on each `load_threaded_request` and decremented on each `load_threaded_get`.
A request is considered known to the scripts as long as `user_rc != 0`.
`LoadToken`s are shared globally and reused if requested by the same path.

That effectively means:
- an extra `load_threaded_request` without a matching `load_threaded_get` leads to `LoadToken` leak together with it's resource (until engine finalization).
- extra `load_threaded_get` without a `load_threaded_request` either fails immediately or causes a later `load_threaded_get` (maybe from other script) to fail on the same path, making the issue hard to trace.

One of the easiest pitfalls here is forgetting that a node can be removed from the scene while loading a resource dynamically, currently results in a leak.
And I believe adding optional argument to this logic will only make it worse.
By example, `load_threaded` first:
```
load_threaded(r, cb)  # Valid, no leaks
load_threaded(r, cb)  # Valid ,second request, still no leaks
load_threaded_get(r)  # Invalid, not needed and shouldn't be called after `load_threaded`
load_threaded_request(r)  # Invalid, still leaks if used without `load_threaded_get`
# while having this is still valid
load_threaded_request(r)  # Valid: starts new request
load_threaded_get(r)  # Valid: ends new request
load_threaded(r, cb)  # Valid: both starts and ends new request
```
And with the optional `callback` argument:
```
load_threaded_request(r, cb)    # Valid, but only if `load_threaded_get` is not called after that.
load_threaded_request(r, null)  # Valid, requires manual `load_threaded_get`.
load_threaded_get(r)            # Required, or you leak.
```
The separate method looks simpler, safer, and easier to document and teach.  
An alternative might be requiring users to call `load_threaded_get` even after the callback, but that doesn't simplify cancellation, defeating a big part of the "fire-and-forget" idea.

## 2.
May you please clarify what do you consider high, low and middle level APIs in the proposed solution? To me, `load_threaded_request` already feels mid-to-low level, so I'm a little confused on how to apply it here.

If I try, with account to point 3, `load_threaded_request` + `load_threaded_get`:
- involves subtle shared state (`user_rc`)
- leaks if misused
- has no real way to cancel or forget (need to finish by user anyway)
- requires manual progress polling or blocking wait

So I'd argue that the current `load_threaded_*` functions shouldn't be considered high level and good for general use.
Also, I realized I wasn't quite right about blocking wait use case as we have `load` function doing effectively the same as `load_threaded_get` except `user_rc`-related part.

In contrast, the proposed `load_threaded`:
- works by itself, fire-and-forget deal, no user polling, no any polling
- doesn't help you to leak tokens or resources
- cannot interfere with other scripts' communication with `ResourceLoader`
- has no risk of blocking the main thread if misused
- can be blocking waited for with `load` function

And that feels much more like a high-level async loading API to me, one that's arguably just missing now.

I see how putting it as the last argument of the preexisting function is cumbersome.

The alternative would be something akin to: `add_callback(filepath, callable)`
```
var filepath = "res://my_res.res"
signal loading_finished

func load():
   ResourceLoader.load_threaded(filepath)
   ResourceLoader.add_callback(filepath, loading_finished.emit)

   await(loading_finished)

   # do something
```

Upside being: you can just check if a resource is being loaded by only creating the callback without even making a request. Could be useful for debugging and it avoids creating a whole new method that does _basically_ the same thing as another.

Downside being: `add_callback` would always be an extra line.

This would avoid the extra line:
```
var filepath = "res://my_res.res"

func load():
   ResourceLoader.load_threaded(filepath)

   await(ResourceLoader.get_on_loaded(filepath))

   # do something
```
... but at this point it'd be a totally different PR.

*Mu suggestions may need an optional flag that lets user decide if they want to only get called if it is finished loading because in most cases you'd want to also be called if it is already cached.*

The issue with `add_callback` is more about `load_threaded` and how it defines the request lifetime (`LoadToken` in the implementation):  
- In the current main, a request is valid between `load_threaded_request` and `load_threaded_get`.  
- In the proposed solution, a request is valid between `load_threaded` and the callback invocation.  
- In the `add_callback` approach, when is the request considered valid? Between `load_threaded` and... what exactly?

Keep in mind that once the request is no longer valid, the user should already hold a reference to the resource, since at that point, it’s the resource’s reference counter that keeps it loaded.

> * In the `add_callback` approach, when is the request considered valid?

That is what I was trying to get at with the last bit.

So intuition would be: The add callback function would work as such:

Dear RespourceLoader, call me when this is ever finished loading and optionally call me if this is already in cache.

So a callback-request with an invalid path returns an error.
A callback-request with a valid path that has not yet been requested may just never get a response. (Could get a warning)
A callback-request that comes after the load-request started and before it is done is obviously valid.
A callback-request that comes after the resource has been loaded should imho get a immediate response per default. I think having an optional flag that allows a user to specify they do not want to get a response in this case is probably a good idea.

Yes, you can technically cause callbacks that may never resolve because of this. But I think in this case godot can warn you about doing a bad thing, but should not try to prevent you from doing it. Especially because I can think of many times I would have liked to know if something is being loaded somewhere without me realizing it.

I can see there are a lot of corner cases with a separate `add_callback`, but are there any real benifits?

For example, lifetimes:
- For how long exactly after `load_threaded` can the user add callbacks with `add_callback`?
- What would two subsequent calls to `load_threaded` mean? They might come from single script or from multiple ones, there's no way to tell.
- When it's safe to unload the resources requested by `load_threaded(r)`?

```
load_threaded(r) # ok, start loading if not yet started, I guess?
load_threaded(r) # does this line change anything?
add_callback(r, cb1) # ok, I guess this should be valid
add_callback(r, cb2) # but is this valid?
add_callback(r, cb3) # and this?
add_callback(r, cb4) # and this?
await get_tree().process_frame
add_callback(r, cb5) # and now?
await get_tree().process_frame
add_callback(r, cb6) # still?
```
And if `add_callback`s all are valid, for how long more can it be repeated? Important note here: actual loading can finish between any two of those lines, or even before the first, or after the last, and that’s essentially random.

For comparison, in the implemented solution: `load_threaded(r, cb)` is effectively: "Dear ResourceLoader, I want this resource, put it in `cb` once it's available", which sounds way simpler. Rest (caches, request deduplication, multiple callbacks, etc) is handled internally. 

P.s.: for checking if resource is already loaded somewhere else, there's `get_cached_ref` function.

As stated, it would have helped me with debugging before.

But anyways. I think my main argument is I don't like adding a duplicate function that just adds a new feature to an existing function. I would like to either enhance the existing function or just add the feature as its own bit.

But this clearly is preference and this is your PR. Both options are clearly superior to what we have now.

*Don't let ~~perfect~~ preference be the enemy of good.*
@fire @lyuma just checking if there’s anything else needed from me on this PR, or if we’re now waiting for your review.

I'm still questioning if the value added by this API is worth the maintainability overhead of adding yet another resource loader API.

Personally, it's not clear to me how I would use this cleanly in GDScript. While this isn't too messy, I'm worried that this creates a race-condition if the loaded signal is fired before the await statement (for example, if the resource is already loaded and cached).
```gd
   ResourceLoader.load_threaded("filepath", loaded.emit)
   await loaded
```

I think I could see myself getting behind this if it's an awaitable API, like this:
```gd
    await ResourceLoader.load_threaded("filepath")
```

Also, while I and @fire can give input, technically we're not the only decision makers on this. Since this is a core API, we'd need to at least get the core team contributors and possibly gdscript team involved to review if this is the right direction to take scripting, or if the way locking is done here can cause issues if mixed with recursive loads and preloads.

Just stumbled across this, so my 2c:

For a separate `ResourceLoader.load_threaded` entry point, rather than checking for completion directly in `load_threaded`, I think it makes more sense to have the callable be an new optional argument of `_load_start`. Then calling the user callback is always handled by the one path through `_run_load_task`. Speaking of, `_load_threaded_auto_complete_user_request` should reuse the same path to get the resource out of the load token as `load_threaded_get`, either by extracting a shared helper or just by making `_get` invoke any registered callbacks.

For an added `ResourceLoader.add_callback` method, I think the only option coherent with the current model is that `add_callback` is valid at any point between `_register` and `_get`, and you still need to call `_get` even if you get the callback.
